title: The Tenth Guru's writings close

cards: Lay four things on a table. A hymn that won't stop praising. A life story told in verse.
A letter that tells an emperor he broke his word. A love song sung in the wilderness. They hardly seem to belong to one person, but they do.
For a long run of days this path has been reading Guru Gobind Singh's writings, and today the block closes. Pick up each of the four, then find the thread that runs through them all.

teach.h: PRAISE: NO MARK, NO CASTE, NO FORM.
teach.b: Praise first. The Jaap Sahib and the Akal Ustat pour out names for the Timeless One: without mark or sign, without caste or lineage, without color or form.
Inside that praise sits the line that recognizes the human race as one. Then autobiography.
The Bachitar Natak tells his own story: his father who gave his head but not his faith, the battle at Bhangani, and his warning that no one should call him God, because he is only the servant.
Then rebuke. The Zafarnama tells an emperor plainly that oaths were broken, and still holds that no one can harm the one the Lord protects. And song.
The ten shabads include the one Sikhs call the song from the wilderness.

teach.h: SONG: A STRAW BED WITH THE FRIEND.
teach.b: In paraphrase: tell the beloved Friend how it is with his disciples; without You, fine comforts feel like sickness; a straw bed with the Friend is better than a palace without. Now the thread.
All four start from the same place: praise of God, said out loud, without hedging. The letter of rebuke opens with praise. The life story is written in the servant's voice, which is a kind of praise.
The love song longs for the Friend. Even in loss, even writing to the man whose armies chased him, the Tenth Guru praises first and boldly.
That's one thread a reader can take from this shelf of writings: not a mood of gloom, not a mood of triumph, but praise that doesn't wait for a good day.

how: Sikhs recite the Tenth Guru's Jaap Sahib and swayyas in the morning prayers, sing his shabads in kirtan, and hear the Zafarnama and Bachitar Natak in katha, the teaching sessions of the gurdwara.

games.q: what does “the tenth guru's writings close” mean?
o: a final hymn added to close the Guru Granth Sahib
his last will, written as his road came to an end
praise said boldly, threaded through all his writing

games.q: four kinds of writing: tap the pairs.
p: the Jaap Sahib and the Akal Ustat

s: it opens with praise of God before it names the broken oaths.
in the Bachitar Natak he asks to be called God
he warns that no one should call him God; he is only the servant.
the song from the wilderness prefers a straw bed with the Friend to a palace without
that's its picture of longing for the beloved Friend.

games.q: you've lost almost everything and you're writing to the man responsible. how does the Tenth Guru begin?
games.why: the Zafarnama opens with praise. across all four kinds of writing, praise comes first and boldly.

practice: If you pray, say the name Waheguru out loud once, in a full voice, and let the sound fill the room; if you don't, say one thing you're grateful for, as plainly and fully as you can.
Then sit in the quiet that follows and notice how the room feels after a word said boldly.

wordCard.voice: The Tenth Guru's writings close. Praise, autobiography, rebuke and song, all held together by praise said out loud, even in loss. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: bold praise. Tomorrow a new block begins: the Khalsa and its code. Go gently.
